To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the immobilized lipolytic enzyme is capable of catalyzing the hydrolysis of all the major glyceride components of butterfat in the presence of water, and that the rate of hydrolysis of each glyceride component depends on its carbon chain size.
a lipase from A. niger, immobilised by adsorption on microporous polypropylene flat sheets, was used to hydrolyse the glycerides in butterfat.

a multisubstrate, Michaelis–Menten‐type model can accurately predict the rate of hydrolysis of glycerides of different chain lengths, that a lumped substrate model can be used for the overall degree of reaction, and that the immobilized lipases are thermally stable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a continuous, immobilized‐enzyme membrane reactor for use in the hydrolysis of lipids.
the use of a lipase‐based membrane reactor to effect the hydrolysis of a complex, natural substrate (butterfat) under continuous‐operation conditions.
the development of an immobilized‐lipase membrane reactor for continuous hydrolysis of lipids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lipase immobilized on a membrane can be used to hydrolyze butterfat to a degree of hydrolyzation that can be controlled by varying the space time in the membrane reactor.
the lipase immobilized on the microporous membrane provides a convenient, stable, and efficient catalyst for the hydrolysis of melted butterfat.
the lipase‐membrane reactor system provides a means to hydrolyze butterfat to a specified fatty acid profile with a high degree of control of the process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a continuous, immobilized‐enzyme process is a viable alternative to batch‐process hydrolysis for the production of free fatty acids from butterfat.
a membrane reactor containing a lipase immobilizd by adsorption is an effective means for the hydrolysis of a complex lipid mixture.
the immobilized‐enzyme reactor is a useful tool for the continuous hydrolysis of lipids.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the multisubstrate model can be used to predict the profile of free fatty acid residues released during the lipolysis of a triacylglycerol mixture, such as butterfat, and that the lumped substrate model can be used for the prediction of overall degree of hydrolys is.
the immobilized lipases can be used in a membrane‐based reactor to hydrolysis of lipids in a continuous manner.
the immobilized lipases in membrane reactors are very stable, and the kinetics of hydrolysis of complex mixtures of fatty acid residues are well described by a multisubstrate kinetic model.
